title: The one he loved (John 13:18–30)
hookLine: the beloved disciple leans on his chest; Judas goes out, and it was night

cards: Forget the well-known painting. In Leonardo's Last Supper, everyone sits in a row on one side of a long table, like a panel at a conference.
At a formal dinner in Jesus's world, guests often reclined: low couches around a low table, each guest propped on one elbow, feet stretched out behind. Your head was near your neighbor's chest.
Jesus has just washed their feet. Now, deeply troubled, he says something that stops the meal.

teach.h: ONE OF YOU SHALL BETRAY ME.
teach.b: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me." The disciples look at each other, not knowing whom he means.
And John introduces someone he hasn't named this way before: "Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved." The beloved disciple. John's Gospel never gives his name.
He appears at the cross, at the empty tomb, by the lake, and at the very end the Gospel says this disciple is the one who wrote these things down. Who was he?

Church tradition, as early as Irenaeus, says John, the son of Zebedee. Some modern scholars suggest someone else: Lazarus, whom the sisters called he whom thou lovest, or a disciple from Jerusalem outside the twelve.
Nobody can prove it. The Gospel keeps his name quiet, maybe on purpose, so any reader can lean into that place.

teach.h: IN THE BOSOM, LIKE CHAPTER ONE.
teach.b: An echo: the word for bosom is the one used in chapter one, where the Son is in the bosom of the Father. As Jesus rests close to the Father, this disciple rests close to Jesus. Peter nudges him: ask who it is.
He leans back and asks. Jesus answers: the one I give this dipped bread to.
And he gives it to Judas. Some readers see the morsel as a host's mark of honor; if so, even now, Jesus offers him friendship. Then: "That thou doest, do quickly."
The others think Judas is going to buy something for the feast, or give to the poor.
And John ends the scene: "He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night."

how: Christians remember this supper on Maundy or Holy Thursday; church tradition honors the beloved disciple as Saint John the Evangelist, while some scholars hold the question of his identity open.

o: Peter, the leader who spoke first for the twelve
Judas, who took the bread and went out that night
the unnamed friend who leaned close to Jesus at supper

games.q: you're the disciple reclining next to Jesus. he says one of you will betray me, and Peter nudges you. what do you do?
o: stay quiet; it's not your place.
lean back on his chest and ask, Lord, who is it?
games.why: he leans back and asks. Jesus answers with a morsel of bread, given to Judas, who goes out into the night.

practice: Let your body lean into whatever is holding you, the back of a chair, a wall, the floor, and notice how much effort you usually spend holding yourself up.

Then think of a person you trust enough to lean on, and picture leaning on them a little, the way the beloved disciple leaned back to ask a hard question. If you pray, rest in God the same way; if not, simply let yourself be held.

wordCard.voice: Beloved disciple. The unnamed disciple whom Jesus loved, who leaned on his chest at supper, and whom John's Gospel names as its witness.

orig.note: Greek: bosom, lap, the fold of a garment. The same word as John 1:18, the Son in the bosom of the Father.

carryVoice: Your line: and it was night. Judas goes out, and the door closes behind him. See you tomorrow.
